new_statements.quote: The Chumashan languages have rich, nearly identical consonant inventories. Ineseño contains distinctive bilabial, apical, velar, and uvular stops (p, t, k, q), apical and palatal affricates (c, č), and apical, palatal, and uvular fricatives (s, š, x̣). All obstruents occur plain, glottalized, and aspirated, although the aspiration is of secondary origin. Laryngeals are ʔ and h. Resonants m, n, w, l, y occur plain and glottalized and are automatically devoiced syllable-finally. There are three high vowels (i, ɨ, u) and three low vowels (e, a, o). Stress is usually penultimate. All of the languages show regressive sibilant harmony, whereby all sibilants within a word are either apical (s, c, etc.) ...

new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level generalisation for Chumashan: word stress usually falls on the penultimate syllable (no Purisimeño-specific statement; the paragraph's inventory is Ineseño).
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'usually'; no exceptions listed. (Sister-language primaries on file list lexical stem-final stress in a few stems — Applegate 1972 sec. 227 Ineseño, Applegate 1973 sec. 226 Ventureño.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, family-wide survey statement reconstructed verbatim from Open Library search-inside snippets (book is IA lending-only). Second-hand with respect to Purisimeño, whose corpus (Harrington notes, Pinart 1878, Henshaw 1884) has never received a published phonological description; Harrington's accent marks as reproduced in Henry 2015 show penultimate and some final accents.
new_statements.identity_note: No Purisimeño-specific statement on stress exists in any source I could open. The only locatable statement is Mithun 1999's family-level line for Chumashan ('Stress is usually penultimate'), in a paragraph whose inventory is explicitly Ineseño (ines1240); it is second-hand for Purisimeño. First-hand sister-language statements already held on file: Applegate 1972 sec. 227 Ineseño (ines1240: 'Stress is usually on the penultimate syllable', with lexical final and some antepenultimate cases) and Applegate 1973 sec. 226 Ventureño (vent1242: penultimate after all rules, distinctive stem-final stress in a few stems). Henry 2015 argues Purisimeño is morphophonemically closest to Ventureño. Purisimeño itself is attested only in Harrington's notes (c. 1,500 pp.), Pinart 1878 and Henshaw 1884 wordlists; Harrington's sporadic accent marks reproduced in Henry 2015 show both penultimate (’ak̓ómò, ’alaxulápù, kšiláqšà, kiláhlə̀) and final (wexáp, xawišáp, wililík, ʔanéq, naxuwí) accents.
